articles.text: Of all the dismal failures in the history of American politics, civil-service reform is the dismallest. The true heart and soul of politics always has been, is and ever shall be, spoils. The Democratic party nor the Republican party could either live through an election, if party leaders could not promise a distribution of patronage. This is so evident that even a child can see it and the spectacle of one party trying to perpetuate itself in power and the other trying to regain power through the transparent cry of "civil-service reform" would be amusing if it were not disgusting.
articles.summary: Editorial calling civil-service reform the 'dismallest' failure in American politics.

articles.text: One effect of the prairie fires may be exactly opposite to what was expected. As is known, almost the whole country for a number of miles east of the Bad Lands has been burned. This drove the antelope both east and west from the burned district and now it is doubtful if those driven eastward will cross the burned country into the Bad Lands. If they do not, there will be far less, instead of more than formerly. It is now thought that a large number will winter in the Knife river and Killdeer mountain country.
articles.summary: Prairie fires have burned the country east of the Bad Lands and scattered the antelope.

articles.text: The Northern Pacific, probably incited by the opposition of the Canadian Pacific on the north, the Union Pacific on the south and the Northwestern to the east, is leaving but little to be desired by cattlemen in the way of shipping stock. Every other detail of the freight traffic is made subservient to the one end of getting cattle through as quickly and in as good condition as possible. Passenger trains have even been side-tracked to wait for stock trains and not a minute is lost from the time the cattle are loaded until they are turned over to a Chicago road at St. Paul. We suppose the principal share of the credit, in connection with Mr. Hannaford, for this expedition, is due to Stock agent Wilson, than whom there is no one to whom we would sooner give it.
articles.summary: Praise for the Northern Pacific's fast handling of cattle shipments; credit to Hannaford and stock agent Wilson.

articles.text: A curious reversal of "the eternal fitness of things" is seen in the fact that there are in twenty-two states, 308,478 more women than men. The greatest excess is in Massachusetts, where there are 66,205 more women. In all the Territories, except the District of Columbia, there is a large excess of men. In Dakota there is the largest excess of men, 29,415. In the whole of the United States, there are, according to the census of 1880, 24,636,963 women and 25,518,820 men. Thus we see that "hope may yet spring eternal" in the female breast for, in the United States and Dakota there is somewhere a manly heart and true for every husbandless female who considers it her "spear to cling." Maidens of Massachusetts, or at least about half of you, come to our arms, that is, to Dakota's arms and help our sturdy pumpkin-rollers starve to death or our bashful cowboys to round up the lean kine.
articles.summary: Humorous editorial on census figures showing Dakota's excess of men, inviting Massachusetts maidens west.

articles.text: The monthly bulletin for September, of Lauren Dunlap, Commissioner of Immigration for Dakota, is at hand and reflects great credit on our worthy commissioner. The following is a resume of the Bulletin: The weather during September was extremely good all over Dakota, pleasant days being followed by cool nights. Dakota has nine stations for observing the weather and from their reports it is learned that the mean temperature for September was 57.26 degrees, the highest mean being 62.4 at Yankton and the lowest, 53.1 at St. Vincent. The rain-fall averaged 1.67 inches, the highest being 4.80 at St. Vincent, the lowest, .14 of an inch at Bismarck. Dakota's wheat yield for this year averages 96, as against 78 for Minnesota, 88 for Iowa and 77 for Wisconsin. Dakota's wheat crop this year is about 25,000,000 bushels, out of a total yield for the United States of 351,000,000 bushels. The Sioux Falls convention, for framing a constitution for Southern Dakota, is highly praised, too highly in fact when it comes to a question of a supposed-to-be neutral territorial officer advocating a measure that he knows is strongly opposed by at least half the territory of which he is an officer. $30,000 has been set aside for surveying 104 townships, the work to done before July 1, 1886. The contracts are to be let by the Surveyor General of Dakota to the lowest responsible bidders. There were 4,547,750 acres of land disposed of in Dakota during the last year, out of 20,113,663 for the United States. The military encampment at Fargo is spoken of and our soldiers come in for a large share of praise. There are at present about 450 miles of railroad under construction, the principal ones being the branch of the Northwestern from Chadron toward the Black Hills and the James river Valley road, between Jamestown and LaMoure. Dakota's first territorial fair was held at Huron, beginning September 29, and was a pronounced success. The stock exhibit is especially praised for its splendid showing. The report intimates that about half the Sioux reservation will be opened for settlement during the coming session of Congress, a consummation devoutly to be wished. Although we could wish that Mr. Dunlap was not so partisan in his championship of South Dakota, we can yet congratulate the Territory at large on having secured such an able and tireless worker as Mr. Dunlap for his present position.
articles.summary: Resume of Immigration Commissioner Lauren Dunlap's September bulletin, with criticism of his South Dakota partisanship.

articles.text: Our market report shows a falling off in Chicago prices in the past few days of from ten to thirty cents. Most grades of western range cattle sold from fifteen to thirty-five cents lower. The best Montana range cattle sold from $4.50@5, the latter being the top figure, except that on Monday some choice 1445 pound cattle sold for 5.70. Far west cattle sold at $2.90@4.40. The combined receipts of cattle last week at Chicago, New York, Kansas City and St. Louis was 83,874, an increase of 7,400, the most of which increase was at Chicago. The receipts of cattle for October to date in Chicago show a decrease of 5,000 as compared with a corresponding period last year. The special cablegram from Liverpool to the Drovers Journal quoted best American cattle ½c per lb lower at 12½c per lb dressed.
articles.summary: Chicago market report: range cattle prices down ten to thirty-five cents.

articles.headline: Cattle Raising in Uruguay
articles.text:
Cattle Raising in Uruguay.

The republic of Uruguay is devoting itself to cattle raising on an extraordinary wholesale scale. One of the leading raisers, recently interviewed, has given the statistics. Eight million horned cattle, 20,000,000 sheep, and 1,500,000 horses constitute the stock in trade of this model but extensive pastoral republic. The export returns show what a heavy customer England continues to be. She takes 5 per cent. of the total exports, Brazil being debited to 20, France to 17, the United States to 11, and all others to the remaining 27. The country is most prosperous and the tide of immigration [steady?]; 20,221 last year. Women are, however, in an alarming minority, and constitute less than a quarter of the arrivals. Four thousand vessels sailed in the same year from the port of Montevideo, with a registered tonnage of over 1,500,000. Next come statistics about the cattle. The average novillo, the steer most used for fattening, gives 150 pounds of jerked beef, 68 pounds of salted hide, and 40 pounds of grease, and besides that there are the bone ash, the hair and the horns. Business is done on such a wholesale scale that everything is utilized. All his constituent parts thus counted up, and allowed for, the novillo brings in $20 a head, while the commission for bringing to the packers, the cost of killing and preparing for market is about $4, leaving the net proceeds at $16. It will be seen that such a business as this is necessarily extremely profitable. In the slaughter houses, called "saladeros," 500 cattle a day are killed. A lasso, one end of which is attached to a steam winch, is thrown over the horns of the victim and the winch set working; the beast is summarily hauled up against a bridge upon which stands the slaughter man, "who with a stab back of and between the horns with a large dagger-knife cuts the spinal cord, and the animal drops dead without a struggle."—[Chicago Tribune.
articles.summary: Clipped Chicago Tribune piece on large-scale cattle raising and slaughtering in Uruguay.

articles.text: Messrs. Wright and Beers have both left, the former to his home in Connecticut, the latter to accept a railroad position in Butte. They have turned over the Cantonment to the sheriff to satisfy a number of attachments upon it. There are a number of accounts yet unsettled which will probably be attended to at the next term of court in Mandan.
articles.summary: Wright and Beers leave; Cantonment turned over to sheriff under attachments.

articles.text: The 13 outfit from O'Fallon creek have turned loose about twenty-four hundred head of cattle on Government creek. As these must range in between Government and Ash coulie creeks, where the Bad Lands cattle Co's. cattle and the 3,000 head turned loose by the Ref. Car Co. also range, it seems likely that that country will be pretty well eaten off before spring.
articles.summary: The 13 outfit turns loose 2,400 cattle on Government creek.

articles.text: We are in receipt of a letter from Vic. Smith, written at his camp on the Meeteetse river in Wyoming, in which he announces that the Smith family is flourishing. Elk, he says, run in herds about their camp and keep them awake nights by their bugling. Mountain sheep are as plentiful as antelope near Medora. The Smith brothers have two tons of smoked elk meat, which they have already contracted at fifteen cents a pound. They will bring down with them about thirty-five elk heads and as many sheep heads. Bear have also been very plentiful and they will bring some choice robes. Raspberries and strawberries are plentiful near their camp. They will start on their return to Medora in about a week. Vic winds up his letter by saying that he will send us a bear head from Billings. Woe be unto him if he doesn't!
articles.summary: Letter from hunter Vic Smith at his Meeteetse camp in Wyoming.

articles.text: It has been so often said that it was difficult to hold or drive cattle in the Bad Lands that it had tacitly come to be understood that none could be shipped from here. This summer's experience has, if not entirely done away with this idea, at least modified it to a great extent. We do not know the exact figures but there have been in the neighborhood of 8,000 cattle delivered to the Ref. Car Co. here this summer. Out of all these not a solitary animal has been lost owing to the Bad Lands. This, of itself, is enough to disprove the prevalent belief, but we have besides, the expressions of opinion of the men who have delivered cattle here, that they experienced no more difficulty driving in the Bad Lands than they would on the prairie, with the same number of cowboys to drive. This is further shown by the fact that the Hashknife outfit have contracted the rest of their shipments for this season at Medora. These were the reasons that lead the railroad company to build the yards here and to expect that all the beef on the river will be shipped at Medora.
articles.summary: About 8,000 cattle delivered at Medora this summer without loss; Hashknife to ship rest of season at Medora.

articles.text: Avoid delay and possible loss in obtaining your winter reading by subscribing for any paper you may want at the Cow Boy office.

articles.text: The party at the Metropolitan hotel last Thursday evening, was a gratifying success. With dancing and refreshments, the time pleasantly and quickly passed away until an early hour in the morning.
articles.summary: Successful dance party at the Metropolitan hotel.

articles.text: Conductor Garlick made the run from Sentinel Butte to Medora yesterday, seventeen miles, with eighteen cars of stock, in twenty minutes. If we mistake not, this is the best time on record between these points, with such a train.
articles.summary: Conductor Garlick's fast run from Sentinel Butte with 18 stock cars.

articles.text: Geo. E. Cole left for St. Paul yesterday to superintend the closing up of the St. Paul branch of the N. P. R. C. Co. All books and papers will be brought here and in the future, the business of the company will be transacted from Medora. Mr. Cole will be absent about a month.
articles.summary: Geo. E. Cole goes to St. Paul to close the N. P. R. C. Co. branch; business to be run from Medora.

articles.text: L. C. Hunt, a recent graduate of the Law Department of the University of Michigan, arrived in Medora last week and will spend some time in the Bad Lands getting an insight into the cattle business. He is a friend of Lieut. Casey's and is now at the KC ranch.
articles.summary: L. C. Hunt arrives to learn the cattle business at the KC ranch.

articles.text: Superintendent Green made us a pleasant call Monday. He was here to overlook the erection of the stockyards. He stated that there are no yards on the road where cattle can be so easily penned as at the Medora yards. When they round the butte at the brick-kiln, the cattle are hemmed in by the river on the left, the buttes and the wing of the yards extending to them on the right and the railroad in front. The yards are so planned that they can easily be enlarged, the need of which we join with Mr. Green in hoping will soon come to pass.
articles.summary: Superintendent Green inspects the new Medora stockyards.
